text_blocks.snippet: Treatment options for type 2 diabetes focus on lowering and stabilizing blood sugar levels, protecting organ health, and managing related conditions through a combination of lifestyle changes, medications, and surgical options.
snippet_highlighted_words: lifestyle changes, medications, and surgical options

list.snippet: Dietary adjustments: Focus on lean proteins, non-starchy vegetables, complex carbohydrates, and healthy fats (such as the Mediterranean or DASH diets) while reducing added sugars and refined carbs.
Regular physical activity: Engage in routine exercise to help muscle cells use glucose and improve overall insulin sensitivity.
Weight management: Losing even 5% to 7% of body weight can significantly improve blood sugar regulation.
Blood sugar monitoring: Track glucose levels regularly using home blood glucose meters or continuous glucose monitors (CGMs).
Metformin: The most common first-line oral medication, which works by reducing glucose production in the liver and improving insulin sensitivity.
Sulfonylureas: (e.g., glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide) Stimulate the pancreas to produce more insulin.
DPP-4 inhibitors (Gliptins): (e.g., sitagliptin) Block an enzyme to enhance natural hormones that trigger insulin release and lower post-meal blood sugar.
SGLT2 inhibitors: Help the kidneys remove excess glucose through the urine, offering extra heart and kidney protection.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): (e.g., pioglitazone) Improve insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat tissue.
Meglitinides (Glinides): Fast-acting pills taken before meals to boost short-term insulin release.

GLP-1 receptor agonists & dual GLP-1/GIP agonists: (e.g., semaglutide, tirzepatide) Injected subcutaneously; they slow digestion, suppress post-meal glucagon, promote a feeling of fullness, support weight loss, and protect the heart and kidneys.
Insulin therapy: Long-acting, short-acting, or mixed insulins delivered via pens, syringes, or pumps may be added or prescribed when oral and non-insulin injectables are no longer enough.
Bariatric/Weight-loss surgery: An option for individuals with severe obesity where surgical reduction of stomach capacity can dramatically improve or even reverse type 2 diabetes symptoms.
